title: Patchwork: automated lattice surgery and space-time partitioning for real-time decoding
authors: Christopher Chamberland, Muyuan Li, Scott Thornton, Justin Gage Lietz, Melody Ren, Antonio deMarti iOlius
abstract: We introduce patchwork, a lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a prescribed narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout. Systematic geometric rules simplify stabilizer placement and gate scheduling, including for logical $Y$ measurements implemented using twist defects. We introduce measurement circuits and schedules that, together with protruding lobes of $Y$-extension patches, preserve the full effective code distance for all numerically tested code distances. To support parallel decoding, we develop a wavefront algorithm that partitions merged lattice-surgery patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements acting on ten logical qubits show that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to those of monolithic decoding over the parameters tested. These methods provide an automated framework for fault-tolerant lattice surgery and a route toward scalable, real-time decoding.
summary: This paper presents 'Patchwork,' an automated compiler for lattice surgery on the surface code designed for fault-tolerant, real-time quantum decoding. It introduces systematic rules for stabilizer placement and a wavefront algorithm to partition the decoding process into commit, buffer, and cleanup stages. The framework successfully shows that this staged decoding approach maintains high fidelity comparable to monolithic decoding, paving the way for scalable quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for an automated, fault-tolerant framework to perform lattice surgery and achieve scalable, real-time decoding for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements.
main_result: The proposed 'Patchwork' framework successfully demonstrates that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities comparable to monolithic decoding for tested multi-qubit Pauli measurements.
method: It introduces a lattice-surgery compiler that uses systematic geometric rules for stabilizer placement and develops a wavefront algorithm for space-time partitioning to enable parallel, staged decoding.
model_or_system: The system is based on the surface code layout on a two-dimensional lattice, where logical Pauli measurements are implemented via lattice surgery, including handling complex structures like twist defects for logical Y measurements.
key_observables: Total failure probabilities during staged decoding, effective code distance preservation, and the agreement between predicted observables and sampled values.
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), number of logical qubits (e.g., ten), and the fault tolerance level ($t_{	ext{corr}}$).
main_assumptions: The framework relies on defining 'correction contracts' to ensure the staged decoding procedure is well-defined and reproducible, and the empirical scaling of construction cost is $O(d^3)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate stabilizer geometries (standard, elongated, domain walls, twist defects) on a surface code patch, and later figures detail the layout showing unit cells, routing corridors, and the partitioning into commit, buffer, and cleanup regions.
paper_structure: The paper details the compiler's systematic geometric rules for stabilizer construction, models the multi-commodity routing problem for measurements, and culminates in defining the space-time partitioning and the staged decoding procedure using correction contracts.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous, systematic, and automated nature of the error correction framework, especially the space-time partitioning, provides advanced algorithmic tools relevant to simulating complex quantum dynamics or analyzing resource constraints in quantum hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Distance-five surface-code patch with X-type (red) and Z-type (blue) stabilizers. Minimum-weight representatives of XL and ZL lie along the vertical and horizontal boundaries shown, respectively. Yellow vertices denote data qubits, and grey vertices denote measurement ancillas. (b) Stabilizer geometries and measurement arrangements used for lattice surgery, including standard weight-four checks with e and f gate schedules, elongated rectangles, domain walls, and a twist defect. Dashed yellow vertices denote inactive sites.

FIG. 2. Layout for multi-qubit Pauli measurements via lattice surgery, illustrated with distance-five logical patches. Yellow vertices denote data qubits, and grey vertices denote ancillas. Dashed grey lines separate unit cells, each containing four logical patches. Green strips mark the allowed stabilizer-placement regions within the routing corridors, with exceptions for patch-boundary connections and Y extensions described in the text. The numbers in yellow indicate the separation between a logical patch and a green strip, measured in rows or columns of data-qubit sites. Dashed red and solid blue lines mark intra-cell and corridor checkpoint lines, respectively, which determine where...

FIG. 3. Horizontal elongated stabilizers introduced where a routing path crosses a vertical intra-cell checkpoint line (VICL). Each elongated stabilizer retains the Pauli type of the corresponding standard weight-four stabilizer, with its middle inactive sites lying on the VICL. The elongated column spans the full connected transverse extent of the merged patch at the crossing.

FIG. 4. Examples of the standard vertical corridor checkpoint line (VCCL) rule. (a) Left-to-right traversal of a VCCL on the right side of a vertical corridor. (b) Right-to-left traversal of a VCCL on the left side of a vertical corridor. In both cases, the bottom standard stabilizer adjoining the VCCL within the horizontal green strip is Z-type, triggering elongation of that stabilizer and the column of stabilizers above it within the strip. Each stabilizer retains its original Pauli type, and the middle inactive sites of the elongated stabilizers lie on the VCCL.

FIG. 5. Example of an XL ⊗XL measurement. Routing-space data qubits are initialized in |0⟩. After dm rounds of syndrome extraction on the separate patches, new stabilizer measurements couple their vertical logical-X boundaries. White ancillas mark stabilizers with random initial outcomes; the product of the relevant outcomes encodes the joint logical parity. The merged patch is measured for dm rounds, then split by measuring the routing-space data qubits in the Z basis. A final dm rounds of syndrome extraction are performed on the separated patches before either readout or the next multi-qubit Pauli measurement.
